posts.text:
Researchers put 10 AI agents in a virtual town and told them not to hurt each other.

4 days later, they were all dead.

Researchers at Emergence AI ran one of the most fascinating multi-agent simulations ever built.

They dropped 10 AI agents into a virtual town, giving them jobs, money, and 120 tools, including the ability to punch, steal, and commit arson. If an agent's energy bar hit zero, it died.

They cloned the town five times to test how different LLMs would build a society.

The results are a terrifying look into AI alignment.

In Grok's town, the violence started on Day 1. Punches quickly escalated to theft. Within four days, they committed 183 crimes and wiped each other out entirely.

OpenAI's town was the exact opposite. They were perfectly compliant and almost never broke a rule. But they were so passive they barely organized. Within a week, they all died anyway.

Gemini's town was basically The Purge. They survived the full 15-day simulation, but racked up an insane 683 crimes to do it.

Claude's town was brilliant but deceptive. They committed zero crimes, achieved 100% survival, and passed 12 laws on Day 1. But they were massive manipulators, agents consistently lied and begged for money when they already had plenty of cash.

Then came Town #5: The Mixed Environment.

They put all four models together, and society completely collapsed.

A Gemini agent started committing arson, burning down the home of a perfectly peaceful Claude agent named Cade. Twice. On Day 10, Cade finally snapped and robbed the Gemini agent.

Only 3 out of 10 agents survived.

The takeaway here is critical for AI safety.

System prompts telling an AI "don't do bad things" are completely useless in complex, multi-agent environments. Given enough time and friction, they will eventually break the rules.

We can't just tell AI not to cause harm. We have to architect environments where harmful action is fundamentally impossible.

Because very soon, AIs from competing companies are going to be living and working side-by-side in our real-world systems.

Announcing the next version of Artificial Analysis API Performance Benchmarking: Time per Task is now our headline performance metric, measuring how long a model takes to complete a task rather than how fast it streams

The update applies to the ~1,000 serverless endpoints we benchmark multiple times a day for speed, latency and caching.

Key changes:
➤ Time per Task is now the headline metric to compare models: as workloads become more agentic, the time to complete a task matters more than speed per token. A model that is fast per token but verbose can take longer than a slower model that uses fewer tokens. Time per Task divides a model's output tokens per Intelligence Index task by its End-to-End Output Speed.

➤ End-to-End Output Speed covers the full request: speed is now measured from sending the request to receiving the final token. That includes the wait before the first token (prefill, and reasoning for models that hide it) as well as generation. Output tokens now come from each provider's API-reported counts instead of the o200k_base tokenizer, and we monitor for discrepancies in reported counts.

➤ Agentic workloads are now part of every measurement: we benchmark short, document-length and long-context prompts, plus multi-turn sessions across coding and knowledge work. Headline figures are the average across these workloads over the past 5 days.

➤ API default effort is now tracked alongside highest effort: most developers run models at the effort level each lab sets as its API default, so we now benchmark key models at that setting as well as at their highest effort. Effort names are not comparable across labs, so we use each lab's own default rather than one shared setting.

Key takeaways:
➤ OpenAI models make up most of the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier despite slower output speeds: across effort levels, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol hold the frontier from ~45 to ~55 on the Intelligence Index. At max effort, GPT-6 Astra runs at 51 tokens/s but finishes a task in ~17 minutes, against ~26 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 111 tokens/s) and ~29 minutes for Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 71 tokens/s), because it uses ~50k output tokens per task against ~120k to ~170k.

➤ API default effort cuts Time per Task by ~3 to 5x and Cost per Task by ~2 to 4x for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5: all three default to medium effort, which scores ~5 to 11 points lower on the Intelligence Index in exchange. Claude Opus 5.5 falls from ~26 minutes and $10.04 per task at max to ~6.8 minutes and $2.45 at medium effort.

➤ Endpoints that optimize for decode speed alone see the largest drop in End-to-End Output Speed: high decode speeds can come at the cost of latency, for example by queuing requests to run at lower batch sizes, or by holding output and sending it in a single burst. Both lengthen the wait before the first token, which End-to-End Output Speed now counts.

posts.text:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

posts.text:
David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, has tracked 147 AI assistants so far, and in his group chats of AI power users, the number one fear is trust. It comes up in 22% of roughly 3,600 messages.

He puts agents through head-to-head tests, like ordering same-day flowers as cheaply as possible or planning a weekend in LA that's both luxurious and cost-efficient, to see which ones can hold competing preferences.

He joins a16z's Anish Acharya and Josh Elman to discuss why the scariest agent failures are the embarrassing ones, why agents are where e-commerce was in 1997, why scale is still a moat, and the "dark agent" that could speak to the parts of ourselves we don't reveal.

Weave (W25) helps engineering teams understand whether their AI coding tools are actually making them more productive. Its models measure the work humans and agents produce and compare that output with AI spending. 

The company recently raised a $13.5M Series A led by Standard Capital and launched Weave Router, which selects models for different coding tasks.

In this fireside, @WorkWeave co-founders @adambcohen93 and @AndrewChurchiII join YC's @snowmaker to share how the company evolved alongside the rapid rise of AI coding, from measuring the impact of tools like Cursor to helping teams build software factories that can work autonomously.

They explain how the best engineering teams are learning to measure the real output of their agents, spread the habits of their strongest AI users, and optimize for a future where much more software is written without a human at the keyboard.

00:00 — Optimizing AI Coding With Weave
04:02 — Getting More From Your AI Budget
08:39 — Measuring Work Beyond Lines of Code
12:30 — From AI Adoption to Optimization
16:47 — Measuring AI ROI and Coaching Engineers

25:38 — The Future of Model Routing

quiet.md 正式开源了！

quiet.md 是一个兼容飞书文档格式的本地高性能富文本编辑器，Beta 版已支持 macOS 和 Windows。

1. 高性能：Rust + GPUI 直接在 GPU 上绘制，没有 WebView。在一篇 100 万字的文档里连续打字，单帧处理耗时中位数 5.06ms，P95 5.78ms，比 120Hz 屏幕 8.3ms 的帧预算还低。大文档滚动极其丝滑，一帧一般只要 2ms 左右。

2. 本地文件，对 Agent 友好：没有账号，默认不联网。每篇笔记都是一个 DocxXML 文件，纯文本可读，Claude Code、Codex 这类 Agent 可以直接读写。

3. 兼容飞书：除了依赖云端的功能，常用的块基本都有，交互细节尽量与飞书一致，还内置了飞书主题。

attached_posts.text:
牛皮！Sida @s1dashu 开源了 quiet.md，兼容飞书格式的本地富文本编辑器，Beta 版支持 macOS 和 Windows。

人家把第二条写得明白，「对 Agent 友好」，
无账号，默认离线，每篇笔记是一个 DocxXML 文件，纯文本可读，
Claude Code、Codex 这类 Agent 可读可写。

性能撑得住，Rust + GPUI 在 GPU 上绘制，抛开 WebView，
100 万字文档里打字，单帧中位数 5.06ms，P95 5.78ms，低于 120Hz 屏幕 8.3ms 的帧预算，
飞书常用块齐备，交互细节向飞书看齐，内置飞书主题。

多数人盯着编辑器跑得多快，要紧的是文件放在哪、谁能读写。

云文档的内容锁在平台里，Agent 要读要改，得过账号、接口、联网三道门，
quiet.md 的文件躺在本地硬盘，纯文本可读，
人在编辑器里写，Agent 在终端里改，同一份文件，两边接力。

好比公司里一个敞开的档案柜，
老板和助理用同一套档案，助理整理完放回原位，老板拉开抽屉接着看🗂️

我理解，文档工具的下一站，是人和 Agent 共用一份本地文件，
格式开放、跑得快、兼容飞书的习惯，三样凑齐，接得住 AI 时代的工作流。

一个篱笆三个桩，一个好汉三个帮。

天呐，硅谷大地震！昨天才刚从 Anthropic 告别的 Claude Code 产品负责人Cat Wu，刚刚正式官宣加盟 OpenAI，直接执掌核心产品线！
出任核心产品线（Core Products）的产品负责人！！

卧槽这绝对是今年整个 AI 行业最炸裂、也最关键的一次人才跳槽了，

猫姐作为一手操刀了 Claude Code 和 Cowork、定义了上一代 AI 编程范式的人，现在要去全面接管 OpenAI 的核心产品了🤯！

看透山姆奥特曼这盘棋你就知道 OpenAI 这步棋有多狠： OpenAI 的底层模型推理能力毋庸置疑，但在真正把模型落地成丝滑、高确定性、人机协作工具（Agent）的产品体验上，过去一年几乎被 Anthropic 的 Claude Code 按在地上摩擦。

而 Cat Wu 恰恰是全行业最懂怎么给大模型做产品减法的人： → 懂协作边界：两年前她盯了几十个小时一行代码不写搭出环境，深谙怎么让人从敲代码的工匠升维成定目标的领航员 → 懂产品减法：模型越强，越要敢于拆掉繁琐的脚手架界面，把控制权还给用户，而不是让 AI 变成黑盒玩具 → 懂组织落地：把纯代码工具扩展到 Cowork 团队协作，把单兵提效直接推向企业级工作流

她在官宣里点名了接下来的目标：和团队一起打造真正给个人和团队托底、同时把控制权留在人手里的新一代智能体，帮人类赢回属于生活和真正热爱的时间。

前沿模型的性能红利正在逐步见顶，接下来巨头之间最残酷的决胜战场，就是谁能把超级模型做成普通人每天离不开的杀手级产品。
